articles.personality_title: New HIV vaccines train rare immune cells to fight the virus effectively
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system, making it hard for the body to fight infections. Scientists have been trying for many years to create a vaccine that helps the body stop HIV. One challenge is that HIV changes quickly, so the vaccine needs to target it in a way that works against many types of the virus.

**What happened** – Recently, three studies tested new vaccines in monkeys. These vaccines were designed to activate a small group of special immune cells called B cells. These B cells can make powerful antibodies that work against many different versions of HIV. The studies showed that the vaccines successfully encouraged these B cells to create these strong antibodies.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows a clear way to teach the immune system to fight HIV better. Instead of trying to fight just one form of the virus, these vaccines help the body prepare for many forms. This could make future HIV vaccines much more effective and help protect people from infection.

**What's next step** – Scientists will now work on testing these vaccines in humans. They will see if the vaccines can safely and strongly activate the same B cells in people. If successful, this could lead to new vaccines that prevent HIV or help those already infected.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New vaccines can train rare immune cells to produce strong antibodies that may protect against many types of HIV, offering a promising path for future treatments and prevention.

articles.title: CRISPR-armed phages help treat severe superbug infection
articles.summary: Bacteria-killing phage viruses souped up with DNA-destroying CRISPR appear to have helped clear up a very serious infection caused by antibiotic-resistant E. coli
articles.content:
Bacteria-killing phage viruses souped up with DNA-destroying CRISPR appear to have helped clear up a very serious infection caused by antibiotic-resistant E. coli

A transmission electron micrograph of bacteriophage viruses attacking E. coli by injecting their genetic material into the bacterium EYE OF SCIENCE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

A man with a very serious infection caused by antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli has improved after being given bacteria-killing phage viruses armed with DNA-destroying CRISPR systems.

The infection developed in the months after the 65-year-old man had a kidney transplant. It led to a large mass growing on his bladder and large open wounds forming on his abdomen.

Conventional treatments, including antibiotics, failed to clear the infection, so the man’s doctors in California asked if they could try an experimental phage treatment developed by a Denmark-based company called SNIPR.

Advertisement

Within a week of starting the treatment, the open wounds began to heal and the mass halved in size, from a volume of 0.74 litres to 0.37 litres.

The man was put on a new cocktail of more powerful antibiotics and other drugs 11 days before starting the phage therapy, so it is unclear whether the latter alone was the key. “It could be that the phages together with the antibiotics had this synergistic effect,” says Eric van der Helm at SNIPR, one of the authors of a paper describing the case.

Bacteria can form thick biofilms that are difficult for antibiotics to penetrate, but previous studies by SNIPR have shown its CRISPR-armed viruses can kill bacteria in biofilms. So by breaking up biofilms, the phage may have made the antibiotics more effective, says van der Helm. “But we didn’t test that.”

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Bacteria-targeting viruses are extremely common. In fact, bacteriophages are thought to be the most numerous biological entities on Earth by a huge margin. They are now widely used on food to kill bacteria that can cause food poisoning, but their use to treat bacterial infections remains rare, in part because of the time and expense involved in isolating phages that can kill the specific bacterium causing an infection.

But a number of companies around the world hope to change that. They are engineering phages to make them more powerful, by equipping them with CRISPR systems. CRISPR is best known for its use as a gene-editing tool but it evolved in bacteria as a defence against viruses, allowing bacteria to target and destroy specific DNA sequences in phages. Now, biologists have turned the tables, equipping the viruses with CRISPR systems that chew up specific pieces of bacterial DNA.

SNIPR’s initial plan was to specifically target E. coli that are resistant to antibiotics, says van der Helm. “But then we realised any E. coli is a problem once it enters the bloodstream.”

So the company developed a cocktail of engineered phages known as SNIPR001 that is more potent than wildtype phages, and can kill 90 per cent of all E. coli strains. This treatment can be given orally to target E. coli in the gut, intravenously or applied directly to infected wounds.

Some cancer treatments increase the risk of E. coli-related blood infections. A phase II trial is now under way in the US to see if lowering E. coli levels in the gut with SNIPR001 reduces the risk of such infections.

In the US, doctors can request the use of experimental treatments on a “compassionate use” basis, as happened in the case of the 65-year-old man, who was given SNIPR001 intravenously and directly to his wounds.

No firm conclusions can be drawn from a single case, says van der Helm. “That’s why we’re keen to explore this in further in clinical trials.” In the meantime, SNIPR has already had another 12 requests for compassionate use.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a promising medical breakthrough where CRISPR-armed bacteriophages helped treat a severe antibiotic-resistant E. coli infection, demonstrating a novel approach to combat superbugs. This has broad significance given the global threat of antibiotic resistance and offers hope for new treatments benefiting many patients. The article provides detailed context about the treatment, its mechanism, and ongoing clinical trials, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: CRISPR-enhanced viruses help fight dangerous antibiotic-resistant infection
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A 65-year-old man developed a serious infection caused by E. coli bacteria that no longer responded to antibiotics. This infection appeared after his kidney transplant and caused large wounds and a mass on his bladder.

**What happened** – Doctors in California used an experimental treatment from a Danish company called SNIPR. The treatment used special viruses called bacteriophages, which can kill bacteria. These viruses were improved with CRISPR, a tool that can cut specific DNA inside bacteria. After starting this treatment, the man’s wounds began healing, and the bladder mass shrank by half within a week.

**Impact** – This case shows a new way to fight infections that resist antibiotics. The CRISPR-armed viruses can break down protective layers called biofilms that bacteria form, which usually block antibiotics. By breaking these barriers, the viruses may help antibiotics work better. This method could change how doctors treat hard-to-kill infections.

**What’s next step** – SNIPR is testing these viruses in clinical trials, including one to see if they can reduce E. coli infections in cancer patients. More studies are needed to confirm how well this treatment works, but several patients have already received it under special permission while research continues.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists used CRISPR-enhanced viruses to help heal a serious antibiotic-resistant infection, opening new paths for treating tough bacterial diseases.

articles.title: Heart surgery cured a man’s skin cancer – and gave him a bee allergy
articles.summary: Having surgery for a heart condition is thought to have triggered an immune response that put the patient into remission for his severe skin cancer, but also caused him to develop a serious allergy to bee stings
articles.content:
Having surgery for a heart condition is thought to have triggered an immune response that put the patient into remission for his severe skin cancer, but also caused him to develop a serious allergy to bee stings

Heart surgery had an anti-cancer effect in a highly unusual case danirom/Getty Images

A man with severe skin cancer went into remission after having heart surgery. The operation is thought to have caused a major reset of his immune system that destroyed the tumour – but also caused him to develop a severe bee sting allergy.

“Something absolutely fascinating is happening with his immune system” says Rebecca Auer at The Ottawa Hospital in Canada, who wasn’t involved in the man’s treatment.

The man, who is in his 60s and lives in Australia, originally had a severe type of skin tumour, known as melanoma, removed from his chest. Subsequent tests suggested he had no remaining cancer.

Advertisement

Eight months later, he was admitted to Royal Adelaide Hospital, Australia, with aortic stenosis, which occurs when a blood vessel in the heart becomes blocked with calcium, usually due to age. During an X-ray for the aortic stenosis, doctors noticed signs of cancer in his left armpit.

Further scans revealed he had severe melanoma that had spread across several lymph nodes, his liver and in his left thigh bone. “The diagnosis was not good, with not a good chance of 5 years,” said the man in a BMJ Case Report.

He was given the cancer drugs dabrafenib and trametinib to take at least once per day. But he stopped taking them after two months due to severe side effects, including liver damage. Later scans revealed the man’s tumours hadn’t responded to the drugs.

Around this time, he required surgery to treat his worsening aortic stenosis, which led to a bacterial infection. About two months after the operation, the man had another scan to monitor his cancer, which revealed his tumours had completely disappeared. “I was surprised, shocked and relieved to be told that the cancer was completely gone,” he said in the report. “I couldn’t hold my emotions in at all.”

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Po Liu at Adelaide University and Michael Brown at Royal Adelaide Hospital – who wrote the case report – have said that the tissue injury caused by the surgery, paired with the infection, may have caused cells around his heart to release pro-inflammatory molecules, such as cytokines. The pair, who declined to be interviewed, added that these may have activated cancer-fighting immune cells, such as T-cells.

These cells may not have received enough inflammatory signals naturally from the body to respond to the tumours, but were boosted by the surgery and infection, says Rohit Sharma at the Marshfield Clinic in Wisconsin.

Two years later, the man – who works as a farmer – developed anaphylaxis to a honeybee sting, despite being stung dozens of times before his heart surgery without a severe allergic reaction. “The new development of the bee venom allergy is particularly intriguing as a marker of a permanently reset immune system,” says Sharma.

More than 70 case studies have previously linked surgery to melanoma regression. A recent report also described how a biopsy of a tumour in a woman’s arm probably triggered an immune response that put her into remission.

“We do know that unusual immune reactions, whether it’s due to viruses, or vaccines or other major changes [like surgery], can really change the anti-tumour immune response and lead to surprising regressions,” says Auer.

Yet, dozens of studies in mice and people have shown that surgery usually suppresses the immune system, leading to worse cancer outcomes, says Auer. This is due to the initial surge of pro-inflammatory molecules being quickly followed by a compensatory anti-inflammatory response, she says.

It is unclear why this man went into remission, but his response may be due to his genetics, says Auer. Better understanding this could reveal the pathways involved, which could one day be targeted with drugs, she says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a remarkable real-world medical case where heart surgery and a subsequent immune response led to the complete remission of severe melanoma, a life-threatening cancer. This unexpected positive outcome has broad significance for cancer treatment research and immunology, potentially inspiring new therapeutic approaches. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful breakthrough with hopeful implications for many patients.
articles.personality_title: Heart surgery triggers unexpected cure for skin cancer and causes bee allergy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A man in his 60s from Australia had severe skin cancer called melanoma. After surgery to remove the cancer, tests showed no signs of the disease. Later, the cancer returned and spread to his lymph nodes, liver, and bone. He also had a heart problem called aortic stenosis that needed surgery.

Two months later, scans showed his cancer had completely disappeared, which surprised doctors. However, two years after the surgery, he developed a serious allergy to bee stings, even though he was never allergic before.

At the same time, the immune change caused a new allergy to bee venom. Understanding this could help scientists find new ways to use the immune system to fight cancer.

**What’s next step** – Researchers want to learn why this immune reset happened and why it helped fight cancer. Studying cases like this could lead to new treatments that use the body’s immune system to attack tumors more effectively. They also want to understand why the allergy appeared, which might reveal how the immune system changes after surgery.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A man’s heart surgery triggered a unique immune response that cured his severe skin cancer but also caused a new allergy to bee stings, offering clues for future cancer treatments.

articles.title: What forest bathing does to your body, and the 5 best places to try it
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You probably already know the feeling, even if you’ve never had a name for it. The way your shoulders drop and relax the moment you step under a canopy of trees. How the breath comes a little easier. The mental noise that slowly melts away, not because of any […]
The post What forest bathing does to your body, and the 5 best places to try it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

You probably already know the feeling, even if you’ve never had a name for it. The way your shoulders drop and relax the moment you step under a canopy of trees. How the breath comes a little easier. The mental noise that slowly melts away, not because of any conscious effort, but just because the trees were there and you were walking among them.

That feeling has a name: shinrin-yoku, a Japanese term meaning “forest bathing” or “taking in the forest atmosphere.” Japan formalized the practice in the 1980s, partly as an antidote to tech-boom burnout and partly to help people reconnect with the country’s forests. Researchers began studying its effects through the 1990s, and the science has been catching up to what most of us already sensed. While Japan gave it a name, the idea that time in nature is good for you is not new. Many cultures have held this for a very long time.

What’s happening in your body

Evergreen trees release compounds called phytoncides, airborne essential oils your lungs absorb as you breathe forest air. Studies have linked phytoncide exposure to a measurable boost in immune function, and the effects can persist for weeks after a single visit. Evergreen needles are also rich in antioxidants and vitamin C, and some varieties (spruce, eastern hemlock, balsam, pine) can be steeped into a tea that is certainly worth trying.

Time in natural environments has also been shown to lower cortisol, slow the heart rate, and ease the mental activity associated with anxiety. You’re not just relaxing. Your body is responding to something specific about that particular kind of place.

And it doesn’t require wilderness. Forest bathing can be as simple as walking through any green space while paying attention to what’s around you. Guided sessions, usually two to three hours with a trained ecotherapy guide, offer a more structured version, but the basics don’t require a guide or a plan.

Five places to try it

Adirondack Mountains, New York

The Adirondack Park spans more than six million acres of New York State, with over a hundred peaks and some 2,000 miles of hiking trails. It is the largest protected area in the contiguous United States, and its native evergreens make it an ideal environment for phytoncide-rich air. Fall foliage and winter snowshoeing are peak seasons. Certified forest therapy guides offer year-round walks in Lake Placid, Saranac Lake, and the Wild Center, a natural science museum of the Adirondacks.

Costa Rica

Roughly 60 percent of Costa Rica is covered by forest, and nearly six percent of the world’s entire biodiversity lives within its borders. Options include a misty cloud forest in Monteverde, canopy bridges suspended above the treetops near Arenal Volcano, a lowland rainforest trail along the Sarapiqui River, or a protected forest reserve just outside San José. Certified guides offer walks throughout the region, led by local naturalists who know the ecology well.

Waipoua Forest, New Zealand

On the North Island, the Waipoua Forest is home to the oldest and largest kauri trees in the world, trees considered sacred protectors of the forest by Māori people. Guided walks are available, including twilight encounters led by Māori guides whose storytelling and song make the experience something between a nature walk and something harder to name.

Matthews Range, Kenya

Not the first place most people picture for forest bathing, but worth knowing about. The Matthews Range in the Laikipia district of Kenya’s Rift Valley holds ancient forest environments with wild orchids, more than 350 bird species, elephants, and one of the only populations of de Brazza monkeys in the country. Guided walks led by local Samburu trackers offer an intimacy with the forest that no guidebook gets close to.

Hawaii

A deep connection to the ʿaina, the land, is central to Hawaiian culture, and the islands’ forests have long been recognized as both providers and sacred spaces. With 175 types of native trees, most of which grow only in Hawaii, medicinal plants like māmaki, and an abundance of aromatic flowers, there is no shortage of reasons to slow down. Certified guides offer walks that bring both the science and the cultural context of the practice together.

You don’t need to book a trip to start. A city park, a trail you’ve walked before, any patch of trees within reach. It all counts. The practice only asks that you slow down, put the phone away, and pay attention.

articles.personality_title: How Forest Bathing Helps Your Body and Where to Experience It
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Forest bathing, known as shinrin-yoku in Japan, means spending time among trees to enjoy their calming effects. This practice began in Japan during the 1980s to help people relax and reconnect with nature, especially as technology grew. Scientists have since studied how it affects the body and mind.

**What happened** – When you walk in a forest, your body breathes in special natural oils called phytoncides that trees release. These oils can boost your immune system for weeks after just one visit. Forest air also helps lower stress hormones, slow your heart rate, and calm your mind. You can do forest bathing anywhere with trees, from city parks to wild forests, and some places offer guided walks.

**Impact** – Forest bathing is more than just relaxing. It helps your body fight illness and reduces anxiety. This means spending time in green spaces can improve your health in clear, measurable ways. It also connects people to nature, which many cultures have valued for a long time.

**What's next step** – You can try forest bathing yourself by simply walking slowly among trees without distractions like phones. For a deeper experience, certified guides offer sessions in special places around the world, such as the Adirondack Mountains in New York, Costa Rica’s cloud forests, New Zealand’s Waipoua Forest, Kenya’s Matthews Range, and Hawaii’s native woodlands.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Spending quiet time among trees helps your body fight stress and illness, and you can experience these benefits almost anywhere there are trees.

articles.personality_title_es: Los beneficios del baño de bosque para el cuerpo y dónde practicarlo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El baño de bosque, llamado shinrin-yoku en Japón, significa pasar tiempo entre árboles para disfrutar de sus efectos calmantes. Esta práctica comenzó en Japón en los años 80 para ayudar a las personas a relajarse y reconectarse con la naturaleza, especialmente con el aumento de la tecnología. Desde entonces, los científicos han estudiado cómo afecta al cuerpo y la mente.

**Qué pasó** – Al caminar en un bosque, tu cuerpo respira aceites naturales especiales llamados fitoncidas que liberan los árboles. Estos aceites pueden fortalecer tu sistema inmunológico durante semanas después de una sola visita. El aire del bosque también ayuda a reducir las hormonas del estrés, bajar el ritmo cardíaco y calmar la mente. Puedes practicar el baño de bosque en cualquier lugar con árboles, desde parques urbanos hasta bosques salvajes, y algunos lugares ofrecen caminatas guiadas.

**Impacto** – El baño de bosque es más que relajarse. Ayuda a tu cuerpo a combatir enfermedades y reduce la ansiedad. Esto significa que pasar tiempo en espacios verdes puede mejorar tu salud de manera clara y medible. También conecta a las personas con la naturaleza, algo que muchas culturas han valorado por mucho tiempo.

**Próximo paso** – Puedes probar el baño de bosque simplemente caminando despacio entre los árboles sin distracciones como el teléfono. Para una experiencia más profunda, guías certificados ofrecen sesiones en lugares especiales en todo el mundo, como las montañas Adirondack en Nueva York, los bosques nubosos de Costa Rica, el bosque Waipoua en Nueva Zelanda, la cadena Matthews en Kenia y los bosques nativos de Hawái.

**Resumen en una frase** – Pasar tiempo tranquilo entre árboles ayuda a tu cuerpo a combatir el estrés y las enfermedades, y puedes disfrutar estos beneficios casi en cualquier lugar donde haya árboles.
